titre: Gerrymander: How an 1812 Dinner Gave Gerrymandering Its Name
accroche: An electoral map so twisted that a dinner in Boston in 1812 nicknamed it a salamander, and gave it the name it still bears.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 26, 1812, the *Boston Gazette* published a cartoon that has remained famous: the map of an electoral district in Essex County, Massachusetts, whose winding outline had been turned into a winged, clawed monster. The caption calls it “Gerry-mander.” The drawing was supposedly born a few days earlier, at a Federalist dinner in Boston, where the illustrator Elkanah Tisdale sketched on a piece of cardboard the odd shape of the newly created district; a guest found it worthy of a salamander, and the poet Richard Alsop proposed the portmanteau word that joins the animal to the governor's name.

## A Redistricting Law, a Salamander-Shaped District

The word designates a very real man and a very real decision. In February 1812, the Massachusetts legislature, dominated by the party of Governor Elbridge Gerry, passed a law redrawing the state's senatorial districts so as to concentrate Federalist voters in a small number of districts, while the voters of Gerry's own party were spread more widely across the others: a division which, without gaining a single additional vote, changes the number of seats won. One of the resulting districts, in Essex County, took on a shape so tortured that it inspired the cartoon. According to James T. Austin, Gerry's son-in-law and biographer, the governor himself found this bill “exceedingly disagreeable” and had laid out to his friends solid arguments against it. He nevertheless let the law take effect without signing it, concluding that it complied with the state Constitution, and by the customs of the time, a political disagreement was not enough to justify a veto, which was reserved for texts judged unconstitutional.

## A Name That Outlived Everything Else

The irony is that Gerry had, moreover, a career far more honorable than what his name ended up designating: a signer of the Declaration of Independence in 1776, a delegate to the constitutional convention in Philadelphia in 1787 (where he refused to sign the Constitution, judging it insufficiently protective of liberties), he became, the very year after the scandal, in 1813, the fifth vice president of the United States, under James Madison, before dying in office in 1814. None of this weighed in collective memory: the term, coined by his political opponents to ridicule him even though he had tried to oppose it in private, outlived him and detached itself from its partisan origin; today we speak of “gerrymandering” to refer to a slanted electoral map, whichever side benefits from it.

carte.punch: An 1812 dinner in Boston gave gerrymandering its name.
carte.idee: In February 1812, Massachusetts redrew its districts to favor the party of Governor Gerry. At a dinner in Boston, a salamander-shaped district supposedly inspired the poet Richard Alsop to coin the word “gerrymander.” Gerry found the bill “exceedingly disagreeable.”

quiz.question: Why does the word “gerrymander” remain attached to Elbridge Gerry, even though he found this redistricting “exceedingly disagreeable”?
choix: Because he himself had designed and drawn the shape of the salamander district, with his own hand
Because he publicly defended this redistricting as a political necessity for his party
Because the text of the law passed by the legislature officially bore his name in its heading
Because his Federalist opponents attached his name to the redistricting to ridicule him, despite his private opposition
quiz.explication: Gerry had laid out arguments against the law to his friends and did not sign it; it was his Federalist opponents who, with the Boston Gazette cartoon, attached his name to the redistricting to discredit him publicly.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who drew the cartoon of the district turned into a salamander, in March 1812?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the illustrator Elkanah Tisdale who sketches the shape of the district at a Federalist dinner; Alsop then coins the word, Austin is Gerry's biographer, and Gerry did not draw the cartoon.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What becomes of Elbridge Gerry the year after the scandal, in 1813?
choix: He is appointed a Supreme Court justice
He withdraws permanently from political life
He is elected fifth vice president of the United States
He is elected governor of Massachusetts for a second term
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1813, Gerry becomes the fifth vice president of the United States under James Madison, before dying in office in 1814; he is neither appointed a justice nor withdrawn from politics.
